stories.headline: Wall Street’s 4th down day as WTI clears $100, Brent hits $107
stories.dek: Thu close: Dow −0.6% to 52,064, S&P −0.58% to 7,591.70, Nasdaq −0.65% to 26,081.72. WTI Oct $102.48 (+6.7%); Brent Nov $107.63 (+6.3%) — highest since May.
stories.caveman: U.S. stocks fell again Thursday — the fourth day in a row. The Dow dropped about 0.6% to 52,064. The S&P 500 fell about 0.6%. The Nasdaq slipped about 0.7%. Oil jumped hard. U.S. crude (WTI) closed above $100 for the first time since May — about $102.50. World oil (Brent) closed near $108. Traders fear the Iran war and Red Sea fighting will keep fuel scarce. Expensive oil can push up prices for gas, food shipping, and many goods. That makes people worry the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again.
stories.why_it_matters: Four losing days plus oil above $100 can mean costlier gas, tighter loans, and a nervous global market into Friday’s inflation report.
stories.camps: Hawks say hot oil forces the Fed to hike. Bulls hope the selloff is short and energy stocks cushion the blow.

terms.explain: The main U.S. oil price. When WTI rises, U.S. gas and diesel often follow.
A key global oil price many countries watch for fuel and shipping costs.
The U.S. central bank. It sets key interest rates that affect loans and mortgages.
A U.S. stock index heavy with tech companies like Apple, Nvidia, and Microsoft.

stories.image_alt: New York Stock Exchange floor as U.S. indexes close lower
stories.image_credit: Photo: Asia Business Daily / Yoonju Hwang

stories.headline: Hot PPI and oil push 30-year yield to 19-year high; Fed hike odds ~72%
stories.dek: Aug PPI +5.4% YoY (vs 5.3% expected). 30-year Treasury ~5.35% highest since 2007; 10-year above 4.9%. CME FedWatch ~72% chance of Sep 16 hike ahead of Fri CPI.
stories.caveman: Factory-gate prices rose faster than expected. The August Producer Price Index (PPI) climbed 5.4% from a year ago — a bit hotter than the 5.3% forecast. That, plus expensive oil, pushed U.S. long-term bond yields up. The 30-year Treasury yield touched about 5.35%, a level not seen since 2007. The 10-year yield climbed above 4.9%. Higher yields make home loans and business borrowing costlier. Traders now put roughly a 72% chance on a Federal Reserve rate hike next week. Friday’s consumer price report (CPI) is the next big clue.
stories.why_it_matters: Bond yields near multi-decade highs can raise mortgage costs and pressure stocks before the Fed meets.
stories.camps: Inflation hawks want another hike. Growth doves warn hiking into war-driven oil shocks risks a stall.

terms.explain: A report that tracks prices at the factory and wholesale level — often an early inflation clue.
The main U.S. report on what shoppers pay for everyday goods and services.
The interest rate the U.S. government pays on its bonds. When yields rise, many loans get costlier.
A market tool that shows what traders think the Fed will do with interest rates.

stories.image_alt: U.S. Treasury yields surge on inflation and oil pressures

stories.headline: Gas and diesel jump as oil stays above $100
stories.dek: OPB/AP: oil surges above $100 amid U.S.–Iran attacks; gasoline rises too. AAA Sep 10: U.S. regular gas +13¢ week to $4.27. Reuters/GasBuddy: national diesel tops $6/gal for first time.
stories.caveman: Fuel got more expensive for drivers and truckers. Oil climbed back above $100 a barrel as the U.S.–Iran fight disrupted shipping. AAA said the U.S. average for regular gas rose 13 cents in one week to $4.27 — in a season when prices usually fall. Diesel, the fuel that moves food and goods by truck, crossed $6 a gallon on average for the first time ever, price tracker GasBuddy told Reuters. Higher diesel often means higher store prices later.
stories.why_it_matters: Gas and diesel at these levels hit household budgets and the cost of almost everything trucks deliver.
stories.camps: Drivers blame the Iran war for pump pain. Officials say reopening shipping lanes is the lasting fix.

terms.explain: A U.S. auto club that tracks national average gas and EV charging prices each week.
Fuel used by most big trucks. When diesel rises, shipping food and goods often costs more.
A narrow sea lane by Iran where a huge share of the world’s oil tankers pass.
A fuel-price tracker that reports U.S. average gas and diesel prices.

stories.image_alt: Oil and gasoline prices jump as Middle East conflict disrupts supply

stories.headline: Europe gas tops €80/MWh as Hormuz squeeze meets thin winter stores
stories.dek: Dutch TTF wholesale gas above €80 ($93)/MWh — highest since 2023. EU stores ~65% vs ~80% a year ago. Auditors say crisis-response goals hard to prove while Hormuz LNG remains disrupted.
stories.caveman: Europe’s wholesale gas price jumped above 80 euros per megawatt-hour this week — the highest since 2023, according to the Dutch TTF benchmark. Storage is thinner than last year: about 65% full versus about 80% a year ago. The Strait of Hormuz blockade still blocks a big share of oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). That makes Europe scramble for other supplies ahead of winter. The European Court of Auditors said member states have not invested enough in alternatives, and crisis plans often cannot be shown to work.
stories.why_it_matters: Thin winter gas stores plus blocked Middle East routes can mean higher heating bills and factory costs across Europe.
stories.camps: Some urge faster LNG terminals and renewables. Others warn Europe may lean on Russian gas again under pressure.

terms.explain: Europe’s main wholesale natural-gas price benchmark, set in the Netherlands.
Natural gas cooled into liquid so ships can carry it across oceans.
A unit of energy. Gas and power prices are often quoted per megawatt-hour.
An EU watchdog that checks whether EU money and crisis plans work as claimed.

stories.headline: DOJ probes Nvidia’s $17B Groq license deal over antitrust dodge claims
stories.dek: NYT/Reuters: Justice Dept investigating whether Nvidia structured Dec 2025 “non-exclusive license” + talent hire with AI chip startup Groq to avoid merger review. Formal info request sent; fines possible.
stories.caveman: U.S. antitrust cops are looking at Nvidia’s big deal with AI chip startup Groq. Last December Nvidia announced a roughly $17 billion “non-exclusive license” for Groq’s chip tech and hired key Groq people, including founder Jonathan Ross. The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter, says the Justice Department is asking whether Nvidia shaped the deal to skip a normal merger review. Regulators sent Nvidia a formal request for information. Nvidia says the deal shows the American system rewarding innovation. Groq and DOJ did not comment to Reuters after hours. Fines are possible; unwinding the deal is seen as unlikely.
stories.why_it_matters: If licensing-plus-hiring can replace a merger, it changes how big tech buys rivals — and how hard watchdogs can push back.
stories.camps: Critics call it a workaround “killer deal.” Nvidia says it is a normal license that helps consumers.

terms.explain: Rules meant to stop big companies from crushing competition or buying rivals in unfair ways.
The U.S. government department that, among other jobs, investigates monopoly and merger cases.
Permission to use someone’s tech without owning the company — and others may still use it too.
An AI chip startup known for very fast inference chips; Nvidia licensed its tech and hired key staff.

stories.image_alt: U.S. Justice Department building as DOJ probes Nvidia-Groq deal

stories.headline: Google’s Dreambeans AI app opens to everyone in the U.S.
stories.dek: Verge: after June tests, Dreambeans rolls out on Android and iOS nationwide. Pulls Search, Gmail, Photos, Calendar, Gemini for shopping, travel, reminders — with storybook-style drawings of you.
stories.caveman: Google is opening its Dreambeans AI app to everyone in the United States. It started as a test in June. Now you can download it on Android and iPhone. The app pulls clues from Search, Gmail, Photos, Calendar, and Gemini. It then suggests shopping ideas, travel tips, and event reminders. It also draws slightly weird storybook-style pictures of you. Think of it as a personal helper that already knows your Google stuff — if you let it.
stories.why_it_matters: A big Google AI helper tied to your mail and photos raises both convenience and privacy questions for millions of users.
stories.camps: Fans want one place for daily planning. Critics worry about how much personal data the app can see.

terms.explain: Google’s new consumer AI app that mixes your Google apps with storybook-style personal drawings.
Google’s main AI chatbot and model family, now also tied into other Google apps.
Apple’s operating system for iPhone and iPad.
Google’s operating system for most non-Apple phones.

stories.headline: Gemini lands on Windows with Alt+Space shortcut
stories.dek: Verge: Google ships a Windows app for Gemini; Alt+Space summons it. Download from Gemini site. Follows April macOS app launch.
stories.caveman: Google’s Gemini chatbot now has a real Windows app. Press Alt + Space and Gemini pops up when you need it, Google says. You grab the app from Google’s Gemini website. Apple Mac users already got a Gemini app in April. This move puts Google’s AI one keystroke away on the world’s most common desktop computers — right next to Microsoft’s own Copilot tools.
stories.why_it_matters: A hotkey on Windows means Gemini can sit beside work apps all day — a direct fight with Microsoft Copilot.
stories.camps: Power users like the shortcut. Privacy-minded workers may keep AI apps off work PCs.

terms.explain: Google’s AI assistant. The new Windows app lets you open it with a keyboard shortcut.
A keyboard shortcut: hold Alt and tap Spacebar to summon the Gemini window.
Microsoft’s AI helper built into Windows and Office apps — Gemini’s main desktop rival.
Apple’s operating system for Mac computers.

stories.headline: Meta launches Muse, a personal AI agent that can email and shop
stories.dek: Meta (Sep 8): Muse agent on iOS/Android/WhatsApp/muse.ai runs in Muse Secure VM; can send mail, book travel, pay via Stripe Link with approval. Free tier + paid plans. U.S. rollout.
stories.caveman: Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent meant to do chores — not just chat. It can draft and send email, book travel, and buy things, but it asks you before sensitive steps. Muse runs inside a locked virtual computer Meta calls Muse Secure VM. A separate “Sentinel” gate checks what goes online. Payments can use Stripe’s Link with one-time cards. It is free for basic use in the U.S., with paid plans for heavier work. It works in its own app, WhatsApp, and on the web.
stories.why_it_matters: An AI that can spend money and send mail for you is powerful — and risky if permission and privacy fail.
stories.camps: Meta pitches safety-by-design. Skeptics ask whether any big-tech agent can stay truly private.

terms.explain: Software that not only answers questions but takes actions for you — like booking or buying.
A private virtual computer where Meta says Muse and your connected data live, apart from other users.
Meta’s separate checker that must approve Muse’s internet actions and ask you when needed.
A checkout tool that can create one-time card numbers so your real card stays hidden.

stories.image_alt: Meta Muse personal AI agent announcement graphic

stories.headline: Ukraine drones hit Russia’s Arctic gas heartland for first time
stories.dek: Reuters: fire at Novy Urengoy after drone strike; Ukraine Special Forces say FP-1 hits on Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas-condensate plants ~3,000 km from border. No deaths reported.
stories.caveman: Ukraine says it struck Russia’s far-north gas region for the first time. Drones hit gas-condensate plants near Novy Urengoy and in Purovsky district — about 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine. A fire broke out in Novy Urengoy, the regional governor said. He reported no deaths or injuries. Ukraine’s Special Forces called the plants crucial. President Zelenskyy said the strikes were justified. This Arctic region holds most of Russia’s gas. Hitting it shows Ukraine’s long-range drones can reach places once called safe.
stories.why_it_matters: Strikes on Russia’s gas core can hurt export income and reshape how far the war’s energy fight can go.
stories.camps: Kyiv calls it fair pressure on the aggressor. Moscow frames it as terrorism against infrastructure.

terms.explain: A city in northern Siberia nicknamed Russia’s gas capital because of huge nearby gas fields.
A light liquid that comes out with natural gas and is refined into fuels and chemicals.
A Ukrainian long-range attack drone said to have flown thousands of kilometers to Siberia.
The Arctic Russian region that produces most of the country’s natural gas.

stories.image_alt: Ukrainian FP-1 deep-strike drone prepared for a long-range mission
stories.image_credit: Photo: Reuters / Valentyn Ogirenko via Al Jazeera

stories.headline: Houthis seize Mocha port, press toward Bab el-Mandeb oil route
stories.dek: Reuters: Iran-aligned Houthis take Mocha Thu, advance to Hanish islands. UN envoy warns “more dangerous phase.” Saudi Red Sea exports already key after Hormuz squeeze.
stories.caveman: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces seized the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday and pushed toward strategic islands, military sources told Reuters. That puts them closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a chokepoint where ships leave the Red Sea for the Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia has leaned on this Red Sea route since fighting near Hormuz disrupted the other big oil lane. The U.N. envoy for Yemen told the Security Council this is a “new and more dangerous phase.” Houthis say Red Sea shipping is safe except for Saudi vessels. The U.S. blames Iran for enabling the advance.
stories.why_it_matters: If both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are at risk, oil and goods can get stuck — and prices can spike again.
stories.camps: Saudi-backed forces call it Iranian aggression. Houthis say they are defending Yemen from attacks.

terms.explain: An armed group that controls much of Yemen and is aligned with Iran.
A Yemeni Red Sea port city. Control there affects approaches to a key shipping strait.
The narrow strait at the south end of the Red Sea — a vital path for oil and cargo ships.
The U.N. body that can authorize sanctions or peace actions; five permanent members have veto power.

stories.headline: Trump: Iran war won’t end until after November midterms
stories.dek: BBC: President says war ends “immediately after the election”; claims Iran wants to sway vote; says oil will tumble after. No proof offered. Polls weak; GOP midterm risk. War in seventh month.
stories.caveman: President Donald Trump says he does not think the Iran war will end until after the November U.S. midterm elections. “I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer,” he said of Iran’s leaders. He also claimed Iran wants to affect the vote so a “weak” Congress takes power — and offered no proof. Tehran denies seeking nuclear weapons. Trump told Americans short-term pain at the gas pump is worth stopping a nuclear Iran. The war is in its seventh month. His approval ratings have fallen as fuel costs rose. Republicans fear losing Congress on Nov. 3.
stories.why_it_matters: Tying a war timeline to an election shapes U.S. politics, oil prices, and how allies judge Washington’s endgame.
stories.camps: Trump allies say pressure must hold. Critics say voters are being asked to absorb war costs until November.

terms.explain: U.S. elections halfway through a president’s term. In 2026 they are on Nov. 3 and decide control of Congress.
The U.S. lawmaking branch — the House and Senate. It can check a president’s war and spending powers.
A global oil benchmark. Trump said prices will fall after the war and the election.
A powerful Iranian military force. The U.S. has targeted tankers it links to the IRGC.

stories.image_alt: President Trump discusses Iran war timeline and midterm elections

stories.headline: Trump warns Iran over Pickaxe Mountain: ‘don’t get cute’
stories.dek: Reuters: At GOP midterm convention, Trump says U.S. may hit Pickaxe Mountain near Natanz; site has deep tunnel complexes not struck in prior waves. Repeats post-midterms war-end claim.
stories.caveman: President Trump warned Iran about activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a fortified site near the damaged Natanz uranium enrichment complex. Speaking at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, he said: the U.S. noticed “a little activity at Pickaxe” and advised Iran “not to get cute” or “we will have to hit them very hard.” Analysts say Pickaxe has two deeply buried tunnel complexes and was not hit in earlier U.S.–Israeli strikes. Trump has threatened the site since at least mid-July. He again said he thinks the war ends right after November’s midterms. Iran says its nuclear work is peaceful.
stories.why_it_matters: A named threat against a deep nuclear-linked site can escalate the war — and shape midterm politics as fuel prices bite.
stories.camps: Hawks want credibility through force. Diplomats fear more strikes without talks lock both sides in.

terms.explain: A fortified Iranian site near Natanz with deep tunnels; U.S. officials watch it as nuclear-linked.
Iran’s main uranium enrichment complex. Parts were damaged in earlier U.S.–Israeli strikes.
Spinning uranium to make fuel for reactors — or, at high levels, material for a bomb.
A party rally before U.S. midterm elections. Trump spoke there about Iran and Pickaxe.

stories.headline: NYT fiction: Theo of Golden holds #1; Moriarty and Patchett stay hot
stories.dek: Sep 4 NYT combined print+ebook fiction: Allen Levi’s Theo of Golden #1; Liane Moriarty Big Little Truths #2; Kathryn Stockett Calamity Club #3; Ann Patchett Whistler #7.
stories.caveman: U.S. book charts still reshuffle under fall releases. On the New York Times combined print-and-ebook fiction list dated Sept. 4, Allen Levi’s Theo of Golden sat at No. 1. Liane Moriarty’s Big Little Truths — a follow-up in the Big Little Lies world — held No. 2. Kathryn Stockett’s Calamity Club was No. 3. Ann Patchett’s Whistler landed at No. 7. That mix shows literary book-club authors and big commercial names still sharing the top shelf as September lists settle.
stories.why_it_matters: Chart leaders shape what bookstores stack up front and what book clubs pick next.
stories.camps: Some readers chase Moriarty/Patchett comfort. Others want quieter literary debuts like Levi’s to stay on top.

terms.explain: A famous U.S. sales ranking for books. Combined print-and-ebook fiction mixes paper and digital sales.
Liane Moriarty’s 2026 novel tied to the world of her hit Big Little Lies.
Ann Patchett’s latest novel; she also wrote Tom Lake and The Dutch House.
Novels that groups of friends read and discuss — often character-driven and widely stocked.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Liane Moriarty’s Big Little Truths, high on the NYT fiction list

stories.headline: Indie Next spotlight: Ariel Lawhon’s Pirate Queen resurrects Grace O’Malley
stories.dek: ABA September Indie Next: The Pirate Queen (Doubleday, Sept 8) — historical novel of Irish pirate Grace O’Malley under Elizabeth I. Booksellers praise structure and a woman history nearly erased.
stories.caveman: Independent U.S. booksellers put Ariel Lawhon’s The Pirate Queen high on the September Indie Next list. The novel follows Grace O’Malley — a real Irish sea captain, army leader, and defender of her people in the time of Queen Elizabeth I. Carrie Deming of The Dog Eared Book called it a fierce tale about a woman history almost erased. Lawhon is known for carefully researched historical fiction. For fall shelves, this is a “who’s hot” pick outside the usual thriller pile.
stories.why_it_matters: Indie Next picks often become the hand-sold favorites that turn into long-tail hits.
stories.camps: History fans want O’Malley restored. Some readers prefer pure fantasy pirates over documented lives.

terms.explain: A monthly list of books U.S. independent booksellers most want to hand-sell.
A 16th-century Irish pirate and chieftain who faced England’s Elizabeth I.
Novels set in the past that mix real events or people with imagined scenes.
The trade group for independent U.S. bookstores that runs Indie Next.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Ariel Lawhon’s The Pirate Queen

stories.headline: Jill Lepore’s Artificial State makes Indie Next’s AI-power warning list
stories.dek: Indie Next Sept nonfiction pick: The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State (Liveright, Aug 25). Booksellers flag Lepore’s map of how a few tech billionaires shaped AI politics.
stories.caveman: Historian Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State is a September Indie Next nonfiction pick. Amber Taylor of Fonts Books says Lepore lays out how we got here with AI — and the outsize role a small group of tech billionaires play. Lepore is a Harvard historian and New Yorker writer known for clear civic storytelling. In a fall when AI agents flood the news, this book is the “who’s hot” serious read booksellers want next to the novels.
stories.why_it_matters: A major U.S. historian explaining AI power helps regular readers judge the tech headlines.
stories.camps: Tech skeptics cheer the scrutiny. Industry fans say history books underplay AI’s upside.

terms.explain: A U.S. historian and writer who explains politics and technology in plain language.

aliases: The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State
terms.explain: Lepore’s 2026 book about AI, power, and how tech billionaires shape public life.
Books about real events and ideas — not made-up stories.
Recommendations from independent U.S. booksellers, updated each month.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State

stories.headline: Alice Hoffman’s Witches of Cambridge brings cozy sisterhood to fall lists
stories.dek: Indie Next Sept: The Witches of Cambridge (Scribner, Sept 8). Booksellers praise New England witchy magic, history callbacks, and found-family sisterhood from the Practical Magic author.
stories.caveman: Alice Hoffman returns to witchy New England with The Witches of Cambridge, a September Indie Next fiction pick. Sara Crow of Crow & Co. Books calls it a delightful return to magic with real history and practices woven in — and says Hoffman remains a master of cozy found-family sisterhood. Hoffman wrote Practical Magic decades ago; that world still draws readers. For fall 2026, this is a comfort “who’s hot” title sitting beside darker literary novels.
stories.why_it_matters: Comfort witch fiction still sells big — and Indie Next love can keep it on tables for months.
stories.camps: Cozy readers want sisterhood and spells. Lit-fiction fans may skip for heavier September novels.

terms.explain: A U.S. novelist famous for Practical Magic and other books mixing everyday life with witchcraft.
A story theme where friends or neighbors become as close as relatives.
Gentler fantasy focused on community and warmth more than epic battles.
A major U.S. book publisher releasing Hoffman’s new Cambridge witches novel.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Alice Hoffman’s The Witches of Cambridge

stories.headline: Gaza hospitals ration power as engine oil and spare parts run out
stories.dek: Reuters exclusive Sep 10: Nasser Hospital rotates outages; one of four generators dead. MSF: engine oil on local market ~$1,300/L vs ~$3 pre-war. Israel says monitored entry mechanism exists.
stories.caveman: Gaza hospitals say they are running out of the oil and parts that keep generators alive. At Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, doctors told Reuters they rotate power between buildings. One of four generators is dead; the biggest two are under strain. Without grid electricity since 2023, generators are life support for oxygen and surgery. Aid group MSF said engine oil on the local market has soared to about $1,300 a litre from about $3 before the war. Israel’s COGAT agency says it runs a monitored system to let oil and spare parts in so they do not reach Hamas. Families say home generator power now costs many times more.
stories.why_it_matters: When hospital generators seize up, patients on oxygen and dialysis can die even if bombs are quieter.
stories.camps: Aid groups blame lasting Israeli restrictions. Israel says controls stop dual-use gear reaching militants.

terms.explain: A machine that makes electricity from fuel. Hospitals need them when the power grid is down.
Lubricating oil that keeps generators from overheating and seizing. Shortages can kill machines.
The Israeli military unit that controls what goods are allowed into Gaza.
An international medical charity that treats people in war and crisis zones.

stories.headline: Al-Ahli hospital suspends key scans and surgeries after generator fails
stories.dek: Arab News / local reports: Gaza’s Al-Ahli Arab Hospital stops CT, X-ray, and some surgeries after main generator failure — including northern Gaza’s only CT in some accounts — as fuel crisis deepens.
stories.caveman: Another Gaza hospital hit pause on vital care. Al-Ahli Arab Hospital suspended key services after its main generator failed, Arab News and local reports say. That can mean no CT scans, limited X-rays, and delayed surgeries. In a place with few working machines left, losing one scanner can force patients to travel through dangerous areas — or go without a diagnosis. The failure fits the wider September fuel and spare-parts crunch hitting Gaza’s remaining hospitals.
stories.why_it_matters: One dead generator can erase diagnostic care for a whole city when backups and fuel are already scarce.
stories.camps: Hospital staff plead for parts and fuel. Controllers say security rules still limit what can enter.

terms.explain: A major hospital in Gaza City that has kept operating under war damage and shortages.
A detailed medical imaging scan. Without it, doctors may miss internal injuries or disease.
Tests that find out what is wrong — scans, X-rays, labs — before treatment can start.
When diesel, engine oil, or parts run so low that machines and clinics cannot stay on.

stories.image_alt: Gaza’s Al-Ahli Arab Hospital after generator failure disrupts care

stories.headline: MSF: aid cuts force mass clinic closures across Sudan
stories.dek: MSF Sep 8: war drives needs while donor cuts close clinics; Central Darfur saw 45 centres lose support in May alone. UN plan ~41% funded; WHO: ~37% of health facilities out of service.
stories.caveman: In Sudan, war already wrecks health care — and money is running out too. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that big donor cuts are closing clinics across the country. In Central Darfur alone, 45 general health centres lost support in May when a partner ran out of funds. Patients then walk farther through danger to the few hospitals still open. MSF says admissions at some of its sites jumped more than 20% early this year. The U.N. appeal is only about 41% funded. WHO estimates roughly 37% of Sudan’s health facilities are fully out of service.
stories.why_it_matters: Closing clinics does not erase patients — it dumps them on the last open wards, often sicker and later.
stories.camps: Aid groups beg donors to protect health budgets. Some governments say they still fund U.N. channels.

terms.explain: When rich governments give less money to humanitarian programs, forcing projects to close.
A region of Sudan hard-hit by war, displacement, and clinic closures.
The U.N. health agency that tracks hospitals and disease worldwide.
A yearly U.N. request for donor money to feed, shelter, and treat people in a crisis.

stories.image_alt: MSF paediatrician examines a child at a feeding centre in Central Darfur

stories.headline: UN rights chief Türk: end Sudan war as drones hit civilians
stories.dek: UN News Sep 7: Volker Türk urges ceasefire and end to foreign involvement. Fact-Finding Mission: SAF and RSF may have committed war crimes; long-range drones hit homes, schools, hospitals.
stories.caveman: The U.N. human rights chief, Volker Türk, told the Human Rights Council the Sudan war must stop. He called for an immediate ceasefire, an end to foreign involvement, and a return to civilian rule. Independent investigators said both the Sudanese army (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) may have committed war crimes. They warned that long-range drones now hit homes, schools, hospitals, and markets far from front lines. More than six million people are displaced inside Sudan; about 4.5 million have fled abroad. WHO also described wrecked teaching hospitals in Khartoum.
stories.why_it_matters: Naming possible war crimes and foreign backers keeps pressure on a conflict the world often forgets.
stories.camps: Rights officials demand accountability. Warring parties deny targeting civilians and blame each other.

aliases: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
terms.explain: The U.N.’s top human-rights official, who speaks out when civilians are attacked.
Sudan’s national army, one side in the civil war.
A powerful paramilitary force fighting the army for control of Sudan.
Serious attacks on civilians or protected places that break the laws of war.

stories.image_alt: Sudanese people seeking shelter from war in a neighboring country
